name: Math-U-See
line: Math-U-See is taught a lesson at a time, by video and a parent. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review are continuous.
description: AMP vs Math-U-See: Math-U-See is taught a lesson at a time, by video and a parent with blocks. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review are continuous.
verdict: Math-U-See is taught one lesson at a time: Steve Demme on video, then the parent with integer blocks, then workbook pages the parent grades [5][7]. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review are continuous. Every answer is checked and sets the next problem, and each problem carries its own hint, lesson and worked answer.

reasons.title: Continuous assessment
reasons.body: AMP has no separate test. It places a learner from their first answers, and every answer after, right or wrong, updates the learner's level in that part of math and sets the next problem. Math-U-See places a learner before starting, with an online tool of yes-or-no questions or a written classroom placement test [8][6]. After that, the learner moves to the next lesson when the current one is mastered, and the parent grades the pages [5].

reasons.title: The problem is the unit
reasons.body: In AMP, everything hangs off the problem in front of the learner: a hint that gives the first step, a lesson with a worked example, a video lesson, the worked answer afterward, and links to the skills it builds on and leads to. In Math-U-See the unit is the lesson. Steve Demme teaches it on video, the parent teaches it again with the blocks, and the learner practices it in the workbook, about a week a lesson, or as long as mastery takes [5]. Across 55 studies, worked examples improve performance in math [14].

reasons.title: Feedback on every answer
reasons.body: After every answer AMP shows whether it was right, the correct answer and the worked steps. In Math-U-See the learner works the page and the parent grades it afterward with the solutions book [5]. Its digital tools page describes no automatic grading of lesson work [3]. Across 40 studies of computer feedback, feedback that explains had the largest average effect [13].

reasons.title: Continuous review
reasons.body: In AMP, learned skills come back in ordinary practice, at growing intervals, mixed with other math. Math-U-See builds in systematic review of earlier concepts [5]. We found no schedule for it in the pages we read. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% a month later, against 38% for practice in blocks [12].

reasons.title: A level for each part of math
reasons.body: AMP keeps a separate level for each part of math, from counting through precalculus. A learner further along in one part than another gets work at both levels, and repeated misses send practice back to what the skill builds on. Math-U-See places a learner in one level [8][6], and its lessons come in a set order [5][7].

reasons.title: The adult's part
reasons.body: In AMP the adult does not plan, teach or grade. Parents and teachers see a level for each part of math and the actual problems behind every number, and each lesson has a guide for the adult. Demme Learning calls Math-U-See parent-led [7]. The parent watches the video, teaches the lesson with the blocks, assigns the pages and grades them [5].

rows.range: Primer through Calculus, in levels named rather than numbered by grade [1][6].
rows.start: Placement before starting: an online tool with yes-or-no questions, or a written classroom placement test. It sets one starting level [8][6].
rows.teaching: Video lessons by Steve Demme, then the parent teaches the lesson again with integer blocks [5].
rows.next: The next lesson in a set order, once the current one is mastered [5][7].
rows.mastery: Each lesson mastered before the next, about a week a lesson or as long as mastery takes. The parent grades the pages with the solutions book [5].
rows.review: Systematic review of earlier concepts, built in. No schedule found in the pages we read [5].
rows.print: Print is the core: student workbook and tests, instruction manual and solutions. A worksheet generator makes extra sheets through Pre-Algebra [4][5].
rows.adult: Watches the video, teaches the lesson with the blocks, assigns the pages and grades them [5].
rows.reports: The pages the parent grades [5]. Its digital tools page describes no gradebook or progress reports [3].
rows.evidence: No outcome study found. No rating from Evidence for ESSA and no What Works Clearinghouse intervention report [9][10].

theirs: Math-U-See is published by Demme Learning, a family-owned company in Pennsylvania [1]. Steve Demme built it while teaching math to a homeschool co-op in Massachusetts, around integer blocks and video lessons [2]. Demme Learning calls the approach parent-led, multisensory and sequential [7]. The levels run from Primer through Calculus, named rather than numbered by grade [1][6].

A learner is placed in a level with an online tool or a classroom placement test [8][6]. Each lesson starts with Steve Demme on video. The parent then teaches the lesson with the blocks, the learner practices in the workbook, mostly alone, and the parent grades the pages with the solutions book. A lesson takes about a week, or as long as mastery takes. High schoolers work more on their own from the video and the manual [5].
credit: Concepts are built by hand with integer blocks, including rectangle building, through Pre-Algebra [5].
One teacher and one method from Primer up [2][5].
Each lesson is held until it is mastered [5].

theirs: We found no outcome study of Math-U-See on its site, in Evidence for ESSA or in What Works Clearinghouse intervention reports. Evidence for ESSA lists it without a rating, because no studies met its inclusion requirements [9]. It has no What Works Clearinghouse intervention report [10]. Demme Learning calls its approach research-based and cites no studies [7].

The What Works Clearinghouse's 2021 practice guide for elementary students who struggle in math rates concrete and semi-concrete representations as strong evidence [11]. That guide is about such representations in general, not a study of Math-U-See.
ours: The two findings that bear most on this comparison: across 40 studies of computer-based feedback, feedback that explains had the largest average effect (0.49), against 0.32 for the correct answer alone and 0.05 for right or wrong only [13]. These are averages by feedback type, not a head-to-head trial. And in a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders that meets What Works Clearinghouse standards without reservations, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% a month later, against 38% for practice in blocks [12]. The test was written by the researchers. AMP applies both at every problem.

AMP's own outcome studies are planned: growth on a national test against hours of use, then comparison groups, then randomized trials. Each will be registered before it starts and published whatever it finds. The research behind each part of AMP is in our report, and AMP is open source.

them: You want your child to build math by hand with blocks, taught by a teacher on video and then by you.
amp: You want assessment, teaching and review in the same practice, with no separate tests.
You want every answer checked and followed by the worked steps.
You want math practice you do not have to plan, teach or grade.
You want learned skills to keep coming back in practice.
Your learner is at different levels in different parts of math.

questions.question: How is AMP different from Math-U-See?
questions.answer: In Math-U-See the unit is the lesson: taught on video, taught again by the parent with blocks, practiced in the workbook and graded by the parent [5]. In AMP the unit is the problem. Every answer is checked and sets the next problem, each problem carries its own teaching, and learned skills return in ordinary practice.

questions.question: Does Math-U-See work?
questions.answer: We found no outcome study of Math-U-See. Evidence for ESSA lists it without a rating, and it has no What Works Clearinghouse intervention report [9][10].

questions.question: Can a learner use both?
questions.answer: Yes. They are separate programs. A family can keep teaching Math-U-See lessons and use AMP for practice. AMP places a learner from their first answers, whatever else they use.
